headline: Ohio: Republicans ahead by 2.8 points under the early-vote model
summary: The provisional call is Republicans ahead by 2.8 points. It starts with earlier Senate results and adjusts for where current early participation is coming from.

paragraphs.title: What has actually happened
paragraphs.text: The source reports 676,836 reported early voting through 2026-10-20. The model uses all methods under the source’s definition. A newly reported ballot can have been cast earlier; participation counts do not reveal candidate choices.

paragraphs.title: Why the call leans this way
paragraphs.text: Earlier Senate contests provide a starting reference of Republicans ahead by 2.2 points. The geographic mix adds 0.62 points toward Republicans under the explicit 0.35 conversion assumption. 88 reporting areas are matched. It uses final historical geographic context because comparable same-stage county evidence is unavailable.

paragraphs.title: Which places explain the change
paragraphs.text: Franklin: 62,337 reported ballots, 9.2% of matched current participation versus 10.3% of the reference; Logan: 4,906 reported ballots, 0.7% of matched current participation versus 0.4% of the reference; Warren: 20,372 reported ballots, 3.0% of matched current participation versus 2.4% of the reference. These places have the largest geographic-context contributions. A changed geographic mix can affect the estimate without revealing any individual’s candidate choice.

paragraphs.title: Turnout can change the story
paragraphs.text: Earlier voting can mean more eventual participants, a shift from Election Day to early voting, or a switch between mail and in-person methods. The turnout workbench separates those possibilities. The retained same-stage history is not sufficient for a supported final-turnout extrapolation here. Explicit low/reference/high assumptions remain available.

paragraphs.title: What the polls add
paragraphs.text: 5 recent distinct listed pollsters retained: 3 Democratic leads, 2 Republican leads and 0 even results among studies with one named option per major party. Studies are displayed separately because candidate configurations, methods and populations differ. Secondary pollster labels and undisclosed shared samples do not establish statistical independence. No pooled margin of error, automatic undecided allocation or forecast blend is calculated.

paragraphs.title: What market prices add
paragraphs.text: 2 recent public contract quotes are retained. Prices are percentages of a $1 payout, not vote shares or this model’s win probabilities. Separate contracts need not sum to 100%. Liquidity, spreads and settlement rules affect prices. No price-to-vote-margin conversion is made.

paragraphs.title: What other assessments add
paragraphs.text: RCP classifies this contest as Toss Up in the captured page. This is a separately attributed analyst assessment. It does not alter the EV estimate or independently validate polling/market signals.

paragraphs.title: Do the outside signals agree?
paragraphs.text: More of the retained recent surveys point against the EV call’s direction. Their different questions and response options still remain separate. The highest-priced retained market contract challenges the EV call’s direction. This agreement check is included in the reasoning. It does not turn the sources into independent confirmations, reweight the EV point or create a validated combined forecast.

paragraphs.title: How much trust this deserves
paragraphs.text: This is a concrete conditional direction, with a wide unvalidated range. The historical EV study is small and has not established reliable improvement over its historical reference. Turnout, party composition, method shifts and precinct patterns are evaluated separately; more inputs do not automatically make a more accurate forecast.

markets.question: Will the Democrats win the Ohio Senate race in 2026?
markets.definition: Quoted Yes contract price times 100. Not a vote share, forecast margin or calibrated probability.
markets.settlement_rules:
This market will resolve according to the winner of the 2026 Ohio U.S. Senate special election currently scheduled for November 3, inclusive of any run-offs.

A candidate shall be considered to represent a party in the event that he or she is the nominee of the party in question. Candidates other than the Democratic or Republican nominee (e.g., Greens, Libertarian, independent) may be added at a later date.

Candidates who run as independents will not be encompassed by the “Democrat” or “Republican” options regardless of any affiliation they may have with the party.

The candidates may be named in the contract for the convenience of traders. In the event that any named candidate is replaced as the nominee of their respective party prior to election day, the name in the contract will be updated and the market will resolve based on the replacement nominee of the party.

The resolution source for this market is the Associated Press, Fox News, and NBC. This market will resolve once all three sources call the race for the same candidate. If all three sources haven’t called the race in this state for the same candidate, this market will resolve based on the official certification.

explanation: The historical Senate reference is +2.2 percentage points Republican minus Democratic, built from 2024, 2022, 2018.
County EV geography shifts the research point by +0.6 pp (raw geographic tilt +1.8 pp × 0.35, capped at ±5 pp).
assumptions: This is a party-margin research projection, not observed candidate votes, a certified result, or a validated winner probability.

The reference pools different Senate seats, candidates and classes. It is not nominee-adjusted; current ballot identities and incumbency are unverified and no historical candidate is assumed to be running.

Historical reference: up to three most recent Senate-election years within 12 years, with a six-year recency half-life. Contests in the same state/year receive equal weight; unrelated candidate votes are never added.
EV adjustment = 0.35 × the change in county-weighted historical party margin, capped at ±5 percentage points. Both the coefficient and cap are unvalidated research assumptions.
Current early voters and later Election Day voters can differ sharply. Individual early-voter choice is unobserved; county correlations do not identify it.
The reported range is a deliberately wide, unvalidated sensitivity range, not an 80% or 95% confidence/credible interval.
Polling, party registration and demographic marginals do not enter this initial projection. No unreported age-by-party, religion, propensity or demographic intersections are manufactured.
warnings: Candidate configurations and survey populations are never pooled together.
Historical reconstruction exists; switch evidence mode to inspect its documented basis. It cannot establish what was reported then.
Latest current observation is dated 2026-10-20; historical comparison is anchored to that observation, 1 day(s) before the requested cutoff.
Survey response shares are preserved; undecideds are not reallocated.
Historical published candidate returns are election context, not early votes or contemporaneous reporting snapshots.
Margin is winner lead in percentage points; Democratic margin is D minus R; swing is change in D minus R.
Matching geographic identifiers do not establish identical boundaries across vintages.
The reference is a final candidate-vote distribution, not an equivalent day or voting opportunity in a prior early-voting cycle.

No recent comparable special-contest history is available; regular Senate contests provide the explicitly labeled reference for this special election. Seat-class and candidate correspondence is unverified.
Historical state Senate returns pool different seats, candidates and classes. Current nominees and incumbency are unverified; the projection is not candidate-adjusted.
